judgements.justification: B's area chair gave a spotlight on their own reading ('a hot research topic', 'will interest many readers') although no B reviewer rated above 7 or asked for a highlight, so the tier sits above what B's 6/7/6 and arguments supported.

B's spotlight rested on the area chair's forecast that the paper 'will interest many readers' in 'a hot research topic'; no reviewer on either committee made that forecast, and the paper's own gains are small.
The response moved all three A reviewers up one point (mean 5.0 to 6.0), while no B reviewer replied to it or changed a score, so B's ratings stayed at their pre-rebuttal 6/7/6.

B's reviews were thin: Reviewer_HkhD gave the committee's top 7 after two hours with generic praise, Reviewer_aQh1 wrote two questions and a wrong limitation, and no B reviewer engaged after the rebuttal.

Only A's Reviewer_7cFv showed that clean accuracy rises as much as AutoAttack accuracy (Table 3 confirms) and that pre-training plus retraining at least doubles cost; A's area chair carried 'the experimental results could be stronger' into the poster.

Both committees saw the small robustness gain and the linearization gap; A's area chair named both as reservations behind the poster, while B's area chair named no weakness and wrote that the authors 'illustrated how to further boost adversarial robustness'.
Every score change (all in A) cites the authors' response; no reviewer moved after reading other reviewers.
No rating contradicts its text: A's 7cFv gave 5 with specific objections, and B's HkhD gave 7 with generic praise and 'moderate improvement', which fits an accept.
Confidences match across committees (5/4/3 in both), and no reviewer said they could not judge the paper and defaulted to a borderline score.
Stage 1 finds no outlier in either committee; A's area chair echoed Reviewer_7cFv, but 7cFv's 5 sits one point from the mean, and its view matched Reviewer_cKPT's.
The verbal assessments differ in depth rather than in calibration, and B's area chair did not set the tier by the mean; a 6.33 mean with no rating above 7 does not explain a spotlight.
B's meta-review cites topical interest, not reviewer agreement, as the ground for the spotlight, and B's mean (6.33) is higher than A's (6.0), not similar or lower.
A's raises followed new TRADES and FAT results the authors ran over five seeds, not copied or promised material, and the raises did not lift A to the higher tier.

added.name: Meta-review dropped the reviewers' stated weaknesses
added.definition: One committee's meta-review summarised the paper without the weaknesses its own reviewers had named, or stated the opposite of them, so the recommendation rested on a one-sided account of that committee's reviews while the other committee's meta-review carried its reviewers' reservations forward.
added.justification: R01 names the area chair's own taste setting the tier, and R06 names different weights on shared evidence. Neither names the area chair misreporting the committee's own record: B's meta-review omitted every weakness B's reviewers listed and contradicted Reviewer_aQh1's 'The robustness improvement is limited'. An area chair can do this while following the mean, so the mechanism is separate from R01.

reasoning: Stage 1 finds near-identical ratings (A 5/7/6, B 6/7/6) and puts the tier split on the area chairs. B's area chair gave a spotlight on topical interest and a forecast of wide readership, with no reviewer support for a highlight (R01, R02), and dropped every weakness B's reviewers had named (new R14). A's reviewers tested the results harder, found a confound that Table 3 confirms, and engaged after the rebuttal; A's area chair carried their unresolved reservations into a poster (R05, R06). B's reviews were thin and silent after the response, while A's all moved (R04, R03). No outlier, discussion-driven change, calibration gap, unanimity argument or unverified rebuttal evidence appears.
